rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The elution window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity tests.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so test a shorter gradient while retaining the optimal first method as a fallback. Holding temperature and endpoints fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness on the critical pair.
The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair near its resolution threshold. Raise temperature at the same gradient to test whether selectivity permits further acceleration.

Test an intermediate temperature to retain the improved central-pair selectivity without the early and late co-elutions seen at 60 C. This may shorten elution relative to 40 C while preserving maximum CRF.

Shorten the gradient one grid step at the most promising temperature to seek a faster method with maximum CRF. This tests whether the central pair retains adequate resolution under greater gradient steepness.

Narrow the gradient window to restore central-pair resolution at six minutes, while raising the starting organic fraction to reduce initial waiting time. The proposed start remains below the estimated first-peak elution composition.

Trim the window further while keeping the slope slightly shallower than injection 6 to protect the critical pair. The higher starting organic fraction should shorten elution, and the endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Lower the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient shallower and recover the small central-pair resolution deficit. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition, so all six compounds should still elute promptly.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 8’s slope to seek earlier elution. Monitor both the early pair for compression and the central pair for selectivity changes caused by the higher starting organic fraction.

Reduce the endpoint one grid step to restore central-pair resolution while retaining the faster start of injection 9. This should modestly spread the critical pair without approaching the time-penalty threshold.

Test whether a much steeper gradient separates the central pair again after an elution-order reversal, potentially opening a faster operating region. Use 40 C to preserve early-pair selectivity, keeping the fully resolved methods as fallbacks.

Explore the fast-gradient region at lower temperature and a higher starting organic fraction to test a different central-pair selectivity. Lower temperature should help retain the early compounds despite the stronger start; injection 10 remains a fully resolved fallback.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower two-minute gradient to change central-pair selectivity and improve the late pair’s resolution. The lower endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition from injection 12.

Shift injection 13’s window upward at the same slope to test whether the central pair separates further in this alternate selectivity region. The first peak is already nearly unretained, so this is an exploratory test with early-pair compression as a key risk.

Reduce the slope while retaining injection 14’s starting composition and temperature to test whether the central pair can reach baseline resolution. The late pair has resolution to spare, and a brief final hold should still keep the run well below ten minutes.

Test a substantially shallower gradient in the low-temperature region to determine whether the central pair can reach R ≥ 1.5. The previous late-peak elution composition was about 0.58, so a final hold is expected, with some increase in retention time.

Return to the faster near-optimal method from injection 7 and raise temperature one step to improve central-pair selectivity and shorten retention. The early pair may become limiting, so this tests the temperature boundary directly.

Preserve injection 8’s starting composition and slope but end the gradient after two minutes, testing a shorter program with a final hold. The critical central pair should experience nearly the same gradient, while the late peaks will reveal the retention cost of the lower endpoint.
Use a slope between injections 7 and 8 to seek full resolution with earlier last-peak elution than injection 8. The higher endpoint avoids the late-peak hold penalty seen in injection 18.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 10 while preserving its starting composition and temperature. This probes whether its small central-pair resolution margin permits faster elution while retaining maximum CRF.

Test a higher starting fraction to shorten elution, compensating with a shallower slope for the central pair and lower temperature for the early pair. Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Refine around injection 10 with a slightly shallower gradient to increase the central-pair resolution margin while retaining early-pair separation. Maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a more robust alternative with only a modest expected retention-time increase.

Test one temperature step below injection 8 to assess selectivity robustness around a confirmed maximum-CRF method. Lower temperature should strengthen early-pair separation, while the central pair’s existing margin may preserve full resolution.

Lower injection 8’s endpoint one step to improve the central-pair resolution margin while preserving early-pair separation. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF alternative, with the last peak still expected well before ten minutes.

Use the final injection to test temperature robustness of injection 24’s well-resolved method; the central pair should retain adequate separation at 45 C. Maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 10 remaining the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
